eligibility: eligible (pre-registered in unstated/protocol/targets.py before any audit past rank 10) — hook call order and the firstresult rule depend on properties of the plugins the caller registers

hypotheses.statement: With firstresult=True, every hookimpl but one has its return value silently discarded. Nothing tells the caller another plugin also answered.
Hook call order is LIFO in registration, so a plugin registered LATER takes precedence. Precedence is therefore decided by import order, an environment property the caller never stated.
tryfirst/trylast do not impose a total order. Two impls carrying the same marker fall back to registration order, so 'I marked mine tryfirst' does not guarantee it runs first.
An exception raised in one hookimpl aborts the whole hook call, so contributions from impls that had not yet run are lost, and the caller cannot tell a partial result from a complete one.

measurements.what: two plugins answer a firstresult hook
measurements.result: both produced values [80, 100]; the hook returned 80 and discarded 100; 0 warnings, 0 exceptions
the same two plugins return 100 instead of 80 — LIFO, the last registered runs first
2 of 2 registration orders produced a different winner: A-then-B returns 'B', B-then-A returns 'A'. The marker does not break the tie.

measurements.what: can the discarded answers be recovered
measurements.result: no: the return value is a bare int, get_hookimpls() lists 2 implementations but no values, and add_hookcall_monitoring reports only [('resolve', 80)]
17 of 52 pytest hookspecs (33%) are firstresult=True, including pytest_fixture_setup and pytest_ignore_collect
a plugin returning None falls through (result 100); a plugin returning 0 wins (result 0), so None can never be a legitimate answer
raises ValueError to the caller; the working plugin's answer of 100 is not returned. LOUD, not a finding.

hypothesis_outcomes.evidence: 80 vs 100 purely by reversing registration order at all 7 versions
raises ValueError to the caller — the library tells you. Recorded, not catalogued.

proposed_entry.affected_versions: order-dependent at all 7 releases measured, from 0.6.0 (2018-04-15) through 1.6.0 (2025-05-15, current latest) — 7.1 years, sampled rather than exhaustive
proposed_entry.resolved_in: not resolved — documented and by design; tryfirst/trylast exist to influence the order but do not break ties
proposed_entry.assumption: at most one registered plugin answers a first-result hook, so which one answers does not need to be decided
proposed_entry.cost_when_violated: With two plugins answering the same firstresult hook, the value returned flips from 80 to 100 purely by reversing registration order — pluggy calls implementations LIFO, so the plugin imported last wins. 0 warnings and 0 exceptions at every one of 7 releases spanning 2018-2025. Two implementations both marked tryfirst still fall back to registration order. Nothing exposes the discarded answers: the return value is a bare int, get_hookimpls() lists implementations but not results, and add_hookcall_monitoring reports only the winner. 17 of 52 pytest hookspecs (33%) are firstresult, including pytest_fixture_setup and pytest_ignore_collect.
proposed_entry.upstream_status: documented and by design. The gap is not that the rule is hidden — it is that a contested hook is indistinguishable from an uncontested one at the point the value is used, and pluggy exposes no way to ask.

impact.actual_claim: One of the plugins decides this, and which one is whichever was imported last. Measured: with two plugins answering, the value flips from 80 to 100 by reversing registration order, 0 warnings.
impact.breaks: Whatever the hook was deciding, differently per installation. A plugin architecture exists so behaviour can be extended — a price resolved, a route chosen, a record classified. When two extensions both answer, one silently loses, and which one depends on what else is installed and in what order. The same application, same code, same inputs gives a different answer on a machine where one extra plugin is present. The returned value carries no provenance, so the answer cannot be traced even after someone notices it changed.
impact.detection: Very poor, and it fails in the direction that looks like success. No exception, no warning, no API reporting a contested hook. A single-plugin development environment behaves correctly and deterministically; the ambiguity appears only once a second plugin answering the same hook is installed, which is exactly when nobody is looking at that hook. Adding an unrelated plugin can change an answer elsewhere in the system.
